title: Governor of Ohio

context.text: This is an open seat: Republican Gov. Mike DeWine is ineligible to seek a third consecutive term.

In the May 5, 2026 primary, Vivek Ramaswamy won the Republican nomination with 82.4% of the vote over Casey Putsch, and Amy Acton was unopposed for the Democratic nomination, receiving 767,360 votes. Don Kissick won the Libertarian primary with 97.8% of the vote over a write-in candidate.

Each nominee runs as a ticket with a lieutenant governor candidate: Ramaswamy with state Senate President Rob McColley, Acton with former Ohio Democratic Party chair David Pepper, and Kissick with James Mills. These three tickets are the only governor candidates certified for the general-election ballot in the Hamilton County Board of Elections list; other tickets appear only as write-ins.

candidates.name: Vivek Ramaswamy
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. candidate Rob McColley, president of the Ohio Senate. Won the May 5 Republican primary; endorsed by Donald Trump and the Ohio Republican Party.

summary.text: Vivek Ramaswamy is a Cincinnati-born entrepreneur who founded the biotechnology company Roivant Sciences in 2014 and ran for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination before endorsing Donald Trump. He is the Republican nominee for governor, running with state Senate President Rob McColley. His platform calls for eliminating the state income tax, lowering property taxes, universal school choice and reattaching work requirements to Medicaid and welfare.

background.text: Born in Cincinnati, Ohio; earned a bachelor's degree from Harvard College (2007) and a J.D. from Yale Law School (2013).
Founded Roivant Sciences in 2014 and was its chief executive officer until 2021; co-founded the investment firm Strive Asset Management in 2022.
Ran in the 2024 Republican presidential primaries, then withdrew and endorsed Donald Trump. He has not previously held elected office.

priorities.text: Cutting the state income tax, eventually to zero, and immediately lowering property taxes, along with reducing government waste and regulation.
Educational reform, including universal school choice, a police officer in every school, tackling chronic absenteeism and merit-based pay for teachers and principals.
Law and order by empowering local police, and reattaching work requirements to Medicaid and welfare.

positions.summary: His campaign launch platform says his education plan includes universal school choice.

His launch platform says he will fight to cut the state income tax, eventually to zero, and to immediately lower property taxes. Acton and other Democrats have said his plans would blow a $10 billion hole in the state budget.

candidates.name: Amy Acton
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. candidate David Pepper, former chair of the Ohio Democratic Party. Unopposed in the May 5 Democratic primary.
candidates.currentRole: Former Director of the Ohio Department of Health (2019–2020)

summary.text: Amy Acton is a physician and public health researcher from Youngstown who served as Ohio Department of Health director under Republican Gov. Mike DeWine from 2019 to 2020, leading the state's early COVID-19 response. She is the Democratic nominee for governor, running with David Pepper. Her campaign centers on an affordability agenda that includes child tax credits, an online prescription-drug platform called Ohio Rx, and a conditional moratorium on data-center expansion.

background.text: Born in Youngstown, Ohio; earned a bachelor's degree from Youngstown State University, an M.D. from Northeast Ohio Medical University (1990) and a master's in public health from Ohio State University.

Taught public health at Ohio State University and worked at the Columbus Foundation before being appointed Director of the Ohio Department of Health by Gov. Mike DeWine in February 2019; she left the post in June 2020.
She has not held elective office.

priorities.text: Lowering costs for working families through her 'ActOn Lowering Costs' agenda, including child tax credits of $500 to $1,000 a year, a refundable credit for lower-income families and an Ohio Rx platform to reduce prescription-drug costs.
priorities.quote: As governor, my number one priority will be lowering costs for working families.

priorities.text: Easing enrollment in Medicaid, joining cities that have relieved residents' medical debt, and restoring energy-efficiency programs cut in House Bill 6.
A conditional moratorium on rapid data-center expansion, requiring companies to supply their own energy and build on former industrial sites rather than farmland.

positions.summary: Her affordability plan would cut red tape to help Ohioans enroll in and stay on Medicaid, and would direct Ohio to join cities that have relieved residents' medical debt.

Her plan backs enhanced production of 'the lowest-cost and cleanest sources of energy readily available' and restoring energy-efficiency programs cut in House Bill 6, while seeking guardrails and a conditional moratorium on data centers.

candidates.name: Don Kissick
candidates.ballotNote: Running with Lt. Gov. candidate James Mills. Won the May 5 Libertarian primary with 97.8% of the vote.

summary.text: Don Kissick is the Libertarian nominee for governor, running with James Mills. A Navy veteran, he says Ohio needs a government with someone who has 'actually punched a clock in their life.' He was previously the Libertarian nominee for Ohio's 5th Congressional District in 2018 and for U.S. Senate in 2024.

researchNotes: Running mates are noted in each candidate's ballotNote rather than as separate entries. Ballotpedia was not reachable (it blocks automated requests). The Ohio Secretary of State's own general-election certification page could not be loaded; the slate was checked against the Hamilton County Board of Elections certified list (Sept. 8, 2026) and the Wood County list (certified Aug. 26, 2026), which both print the three tickets (Acton/Pepper, Ramaswamy/McColley, Kissick/Mills) and list other tickets only as write-ins. Write-in tickets (e.g., Timothy Grady, Heather Hill, Renea Turner) are not included. Neither Ramaswamy nor Acton has held elected office, so no record items are listed. No direct source on abortion or guns was found for either major candidate, so those positions are omitted. Little public material was found for Don Kissick beyond a short interview; his campaign site was not reachable.
